# Python in Giotto Suite

Giotto Suite needs no Python setup. The few functions that wrap a Python tool
install that tool the first time they run, in an environment of its own, and
reuse it afterwards. Python never starts in your R session: each tool runs in
a separate worker R session (`GiottoUtils::py_run()`), so tools that need
different Python or package versions work side by side in one analysis.

The environments are built by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) through
[reticulate](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/)'s `py_require()`; reticulate
1.41 or later is needed. Nothing else, and no conda, is required.

# Functions that use Python

| Function | Python tool |
| --- | --- |
| `doCellposeSegmentation()` | cellpose |
| `doMesmerSegmentation()`, `doCellSegmentation()` | deepcell (Mesmer) |
| `doStardistSegmentation()` | StarDist |
| `preprocessImageToMatrix()`, `estimateAutomatedImageRegistrationWithSIFT()` | scikit-image |
| `to_simple_tif()`, `tif_metadata()` (for formats without XML metadata) | tifffile |
| `runONTraCV1()` | ONTraC 1.x |
| `GiottoConnect::runScrublet()` | Scrublet |
| `GiottoConnect::runONTraC()` | ONTraC |

`giottoToAnndataZarr()` still uses its own environment through basilisk.

The first call of a tool needs internet and takes longer, since its packages
are downloaded; deep learning tools such as cellpose and StarDist download
several hundred megabytes. Later calls start in about a second.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(Giotto)

# nothing to install first: the first call installs cellpose
doCellposeSegmentation(
    input = "dapi.tif",
    mask_output = "dapi_mask.tif",
    model_name = "nuclei"
)
```

# Using your own Python

To run tools with a Python installation you manage yourself, for example for a
fixed, validated set of versions, point Giotto to it. Its packages are then
yours to install; nothing is installed into it.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# one Python for every tool
options(giotto.py_python = "/path/to/venv/bin/python")

# or one per tool, by the tool's name; other tools keep their own environment
options(giotto.py_python = list(
    cellpose = "/path/to/cellpose-env/bin/python"
))
```

The segmentation functions also take the path directly, as `python_env`.

# Offline use and HPC

On a cluster whose compute nodes have no internet, run each tool once on a node
that has internet, with the uv cache on shared storage, then switch downloads
off on the compute nodes:

```sh
# on a login node with internet: run each tool once
export UV_CACHE_DIR=/shared/storage/uv-cache

# on the compute nodes
export UV_CACHE_DIR=/shared/storage/uv-cache
export UV_OFFLINE=1
```

A tool whose packages are not in the cache then stops with a message saying
so.

# Versions and troubleshooting

The Python version and the version of each package a tool used are returned
with its result, and GiottoConnect tools store them with their parameters in
the giotto object.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
res <- GiottoUtils::py_run(
    function() reticulate::import("numpy")$`__version__`,
    requirements = "numpy"
)
attr(res, "py_versions")

# run a tool in this R session instead of a worker, e.g. to debug it
options(giotto.py_isolate = FALSE)
```

An error in a tool is returned as one R error with the tool's Python message.
For an own Python, a missing package is named in the error.
